summary.text: Take \(n=2^{14}\cdot 4409\cdot 458009\), with \(4409\) and \(458009\) prime; multiplicativity gives \(\sigma(n)=66{,}183{,}576{,}284{,}700\) and \(\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)=132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}399\). Thus the deficiency sum is \(2\sigma(n)-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)=1\), although \(n\) is neither \(1\) nor \(12\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(\sigma(m)=\sum_{e\mid m}e\) denote the sum of the positive divisors of \(m\). The deficiency used in the definition of A296075 is
\[
\delta(m)=2m-\sigma(m),
\]
so
\[
a(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\delta(d)=\sum_{d\mid n}\bigl(2d-\sigma(d)\bigr).
\]
We will exhibit a positive integer other than \(1\) and \(12\) for which this sum is \(1\).

Take
\[
N=2^{14}\cdot 4409\cdot 458009
  =33{,}085{,}221{,}781{,}504.
\]
We first record that the displayed factorization is into pairwise coprime prime powers. The only non-immediate points are the primality of \(4409\) and \(458009\); here is a concise primality check.

We use the following standard order criterion. Suppose \(m>1\), the complete prime factorization of \(m-1\) is known, and there is an integer \(b\) such that
\[
b^{m-1}\equiv 1\pmod m
\]
and, for every prime \(r\mid m-1\),
\[
\gcd\bigl(b^{(m-1)/r}-1,m\bigr)=1.
\]
Then \(m\) is prime. Indeed, if \(q\) is any prime divisor of \(m\), the first congruence shows that the order of \(b\) modulo \(q\) divides \(m-1\). The gcd conditions show, one prime factor at a time and with the full multiplicities occurring in \(m-1\), that this order cannot divide \((m-1)/r\) for any prime \(r\mid m-1\). Hence the order is exactly \(m-1\). Since an order modulo the prime \(q\) divides \(q-1\), we get \(m-1\mid q-1\), and consequently \(q\ge m\). As \(q\mid m\), this forces \(q=m\), so \(m\) is prime.

The small primes \(2,3,5,19,29\) are immediate by trial division. The following modular computations, all obtainable by repeated squaring, apply the criterion successively.

First,
\[
229-1=228=2^2\cdot3\cdot19.
\]
With base \(6\),
\[
6^{228}\equiv1\pmod{229},
\]
and the powers corresponding to the distinct prime factors of \(228\) are
\[
6^{228/2}\equiv228,
\qquad
6^{228/3}\equiv134,
\qquad
6^{228/19}\equiv165
\pmod{229}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\gcd(228-1,229)=
\gcd(134-1,229)=
\gcd(165-1,229)=1.
\]
Thus \(229\) is prime.

Next,
\[
57251-1=57250=2\cdot5^3\cdot229.
\]
With base \(2\),
\[
2^{57250}\equiv1\pmod{57251},
\]
and
\[
2^{57250/2}\equiv57250,
\qquad
2^{57250/5}\equiv55371,
\qquad
2^{57250/229}\equiv48088
\pmod{57251}.
\]
The corresponding gcds are
\[
\gcd(57250-1,57251)=
\gcd(55371-1,57251)=
\gcd(48088-1,57251)=1.
\]
Therefore \(57251\) is prime.

For \(4409\), we have
\[
4409-1=4408=2^3\cdot19\cdot29.
\]
Using base \(3\), modular exponentiation gives
\[
3^{4408}\equiv1\pmod{4409}
\]
and
\[
3^{4408/2}\equiv4408,
\qquad
3^{4408/19}\equiv209,
\qquad
3^{4408/29}\equiv3965
\pmod{4409}.
\]
Also,
\[
\gcd(4408-1,4409)=
\gcd(209-1,4409)=
\gcd(3965-1,4409)=1.
\]
Hence \(4409\) is prime.

Finally,
\[
458009-1=458008=2^3\cdot57251.
\]
Again with base \(3\),
\[
3^{458008}\equiv1\pmod{458009},
\]
while
\[
3^{458008/2}\equiv458008,
\qquad
3^{458008/57251}\equiv6561
\pmod{458009}.
\]
Here
\[
\gcd(458008-1,458009)=1
\quad\text{and}\quad
\gcd(6561-1,458009)=\gcd(6560,458009)=1.
\]
Thus \(458009\) is prime. In particular, the three numbers \(2^{14}\), \(4409\), and \(458009\) are pairwise coprime.

We now evaluate \(a(N)\) without listing all divisors individually. Separating the two terms in its definition gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
 &=2\sum_{d\mid n}d-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\\
 &=2\sigma(n)-S(n),
\end{aligned}
\]
where we have put
\[
S(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d).
\]
Both \(\sigma\) and \(S\) are multiplicative on coprime arguments. For \(\sigma\), this follows because if \(\gcd(u,v)=1\), every divisor of \(uv\) is uniquely of the form \(xy\) with \(x\mid u\) and \(y\mid v\); hence
\[
\sigma(uv)=\sum_{x\mid u}\sum_{y\mid v}xy
          =\sigma(u)\sigma(v).
\]
The same divisor decomposition, together with multiplicativity of \(\sigma\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(uv)
 &=\sum_{d\mid uv}\sigma(d)
  =\sum_{x\mid u}\sum_{y\mid v}\sigma(xy)\\
 &=\sum_{x\mid u}\sum_{y\mid v}\sigma(x)\sigma(y)
  =S(u)S(v)
\end{aligned}
\]
whenever \(u\) and \(v\) are coprime.

For the power of \(2\), the geometric-series formula gives
\[
\sigma(2^{14})=1+2+\cdots+2^{14}=2^{15}-1=32767.
\]
For a prime \(p\), \(\sigma(p)=1+p\). Therefore
\[
\sigma(4409)=4410,
\qquad
\sigma(458009)=458010.
\]
By multiplicativity,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma(N)
 &=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010\\
 &=66{,}183{,}576{,}284{,}700.
\end{aligned}
\]

It remains to evaluate \(S\) on the same three prime-power factors. For \(2^{14}\), its divisors are \(2^j\), \(0\le j\le14\), and
\[
\sigma(2^j)=1+2+\cdots+2^j=2^{j+1}-1.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(2^{14})
 &=\sum_{j=0}^{14}(2^{j+1}-1)\\
 &=\left(2+4+\cdots+2^{15}\right)-15\\
 &=2(2^{15}-1)-15\\
 &=65519.
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(p\) is prime, its only divisors are \(1\) and \(p\), so
\[
S(p)=\sigma(1)+\sigma(p)=1+(p+1)=p+2.
\]
Thus
\[
S(4409)=4411,
\qquad
S(458009)=458011.
\]
Using multiplicativity once more,
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(N)
 &=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011\\
 &=132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}399.
\end{aligned}
\]
For completeness, the intermediate products are
\[
32767\cdot4410=144{,}502{,}470,
\qquad
65519\cdot4411=289{,}004{,}309,
\]
which yield the two displayed large products after multiplication by \(458010\) and \(458011\), respectively.

Substitution into \(a(N)=2\sigma(N)-S(N)\) now gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(N)
 &=2\cdot66{,}183{,}576{,}284{,}700
   -132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}399\\
 &=132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}400
   -132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}399\\
 &=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
But
\[
N=33{,}085{,}221{,}781{,}504

e1,12.
\]
Thus \(N\) is a positive integer distinct from both proposed solutions, yet \(a(N)=1\). This is a counterexample to the assertion that, for every positive integer \(n\), one has \(a(n)=1\) if and only if \(n=1\) or \(n=12\). Therefore the conjecture is false.
